options.label: An animal that always stays warm from its own body heat
options.feedback: That is an endotherm (like a mammal or bird). An ectotherm gets its heat from outside its body.

options.label: An animal whose body temperature depends on the surrounding environment
options.feedback: Correct. Ectotherms like reptiles and amphibians rely on external heat sources such as the sun or warm ground.

options.label: An animal that can choose its body temperature at will
options.feedback: No animal can simply choose its temperature; ectotherms must move to warmer or cooler places to adjust it.

options.label: An animal that has no body temperature at all
options.feedback: Every animal has some body temperature. Ectotherms just cannot regulate it internally like warm-blooded animals.

items.ok_line: Ectotherm means 'outside heat'—body temperature follows the surroundings.
items.ko_line: Reptiles and amphibians do not make their own body heat internally.
items.exp_text: An ectotherm is an animal that gains body heat from its environment rather than generating it internally. Lizards warm up by basking, frogs warm up by sitting on warm rocks. Their internal temperature rises and falls with the air, water, or ground around them.

items.prompt: Which of these animals is an endotherm?

options.label: A snake
options.feedback: Snakes are ectotherms; they warm up by basking, not by internal heat production.

options.label: A frog
options.feedback: Frogs are ectotherms too; they depend on their surroundings for body heat.

options.label: A turtle
options.feedback: Turtles are ectotherms; they must bask to raise their body temperature.

options.label: A cat
options.feedback: Correct. Cats, like all mammals, are endotherms—they produce their own body heat internally and stay warm regardless of outside temperature.

items.ok_line: Mammals and birds are endotherms; reptiles and amphibians are ectotherms.
items.ko_line: The cold-blooded animals here all rely on external heat.
items.exp_text: Endotherms are animals that generate body heat from within, such as mammals and birds. A cat produces its own warmth continuously. In contrast, a snake, frog, or turtle belongs to the ectotherm group, warming up only when its environment does.

items.prompt: What happens to a lizard's body temperature on a cold night?

options.label: It stays the same as during the day
options.feedback: It cannot, because the lizard has no internal heater; at night the air cools and the lizard cools with it.

options.label: It rises slightly to keep the lizard active
options.feedback: Cold nights cool the environment, so an ectotherm's temperature falls, not rises.

options.label: It drops close to the air temperature around it
options.feedback: Correct. An ectotherm's body temperature mirrors its surroundings, so on a cold night the lizard becomes cold too.

options.label: It stops being measured because the lizard is asleep
options.feedback: The lizard still has a body temperature even when asleep; it simply matches the cold of the night.

items.ok_line: Ectotherms cool down when their environment cools.
items.ko_line: A lizard cannot keep itself warm overnight.
items.exp_text: Reptiles are ectotherms, so their body temperature follows the air temperature. On a cold night the air cools, the lizard's body cools with it, and its activity slows down. It must wait for the morning sun to warm it back up.

items.prompt: Why does a cold lizard move slowly?

options.label: Its muscles work poorly when they are cold
options.feedback: Correct. Muscle contractions depend on chemical reactions that run slowly at low temperatures, so cold muscles are weak and sluggish.

options.label: It is tired from basking all day
options.feedback: Basking warms and energizes a lizard; coldness itself slows its movements, not tiredness.

options.label: It has no reason to move fast at night
options.feedback: Speed is not about motivation; the lizard's cold body simply cannot move quickly.

options.label: Its brain tells it to be cautious
options.feedback: Caution does not cause slow movement; the physical effect of cold on muscles is what limits speed.

items.ok_line: Cold slows the chemical reactions inside muscle cells.
items.ko_line: The lizard is not choosing to be slow—it physically cannot go fast.
items.exp_text: Muscles work by chemical reactions that need heat to run at full speed. When a lizard is cold, those reactions slow down, making its muscles weak and sluggish. That is why a chilled lizard cannot run fast or dart away quickly.

items.prompt: What does a lizard do when its body gets too warm from basking?

options.label: It keeps basking so the heat spreads evenly
options.feedback: Keeping basking would overheat it. The lizard must move away from the heat source to cool down.

options.label: It drinks more water to cool down
options.feedback: Drinking does not cool an ectotherm directly; moving to shade is how a lizard lowers its temperature.

options.label: It runs very fast to make its own heat
options.feedback: Running generates heat, which would make the lizard hotter, not cooler.

options.label: It moves into the shade or a burrow
options.feedback: Correct. By leaving the sun and finding shade or a cool hiding spot, the lizard lets its body cool to the lower air temperature.

items.ok_line: Lizards seek shade to drop their temperature.
items.ko_line: The lizard must actively move to a cooler place.
items.exp_text: An ectotherm controls its temperature by behavior. When a lizard gets too hot from basking, it simply moves into shade, underground, or a cooler crevice. There, its body temperature falls as the surroundings are cooler.

options.label: A type of deep sleep that lasts for years
options.feedback: Brumation is a seasonal dormancy that lasts through winter, not years. Most reptiles emerge after a few months.

options.label: A way reptiles pant to cool down
options.feedback: Panting cools, whereas brumation is a cold-weather slowdown where the animal is inactive and does not eat.

options.label: A winter period when a reptile's body slows down and it barely moves
options.feedback: Correct. Brumation is the reptile version of hibernation; the animal becomes sluggish, its heart rate drops, and it stops eating until warmth returns.

options.label: A summer dormancy to avoid heat
options.feedback: That is estivation, not brumation. Brumation happens in cold winter months.

items.ok_line: Brumation is a reptile's cold-weather slowdown.
items.ko_line: The cool season triggers brumation, not the hot one.
items.exp_text: Brumation is a state of reduced activity and metabolism that reptiles enter during cold winters. The animal finds a sheltered spot, its heart rate and breathing slow, and it uses stored energy instead of eating. It revives when temperatures rise in spring.

items.prompt: Which part of a reptile's body controls its heart rate on warm versus cold days?

options.label: Its skin, which absorbs more heat on warm days
options.feedback: The skin absorbs heat, but the heart rate is not controlled by the skin; it responds to the animal's overall body temperature.

options.label: Its body temperature, which changes with the surroundings
options.feedback: Correct. A reptile's heart beats faster when the body is warm and slower when the body is cold, because chemical reactions speed up or slow down with temperature.

options.label: Its brain, which decides how fast to beat
options.feedback: The brain does not make a conscious choice; the heart rate follows body temperature automatically.

options.label: Its stomach, which needs more blood after eating
options.feedback: Digestion can affect heart rate, but the main driver for warm versus cold days is body temperature itself.

items.ok_line: A warmer body makes the heart beat faster.
items.ko_line: The heart rate simply follows the animal's temperature.
items.exp_text: In ectotherms, all internal processes, including heart rate, are temperature-dependent. When a reptile warms up, its heart beats faster to move blood and oxygen quickly. When it cools down, the heart slows dramatically, matching the sluggish body.

items.prompt: Why does a lizard's skin darken after a cold night?

options.label: Darker skin absorbs more sunlight, helping it warm faster
options.feedback: Correct. Dark colors absorb more solar energy than light ones, so a darker lizard heats up more quickly in morning sun.

options.label: The cold makes its pigment cells shrink
options.feedback: Cold causes the pigment cells to spread out, darkening the skin, not shrink. And the purpose is heat absorption.

options.label: It is a sign of illness from the cold
options.feedback: Darkening is a normal response to cold, not a sickness, and it helps the lizard warm up.

options.label: Its skin loses color because blood flow decreases
options.feedback: Blood flow changes, but darkening is caused by pigment movement in skin cells to absorb more heat.

items.ok_line: Darker skin traps more warmth from the sun.
items.ko_line: This is a normal way to speed up warming.
items.exp_text: Many lizards can change skin color by spreading or gathering pigment in their skin cells. After a cold night, they darken their skin so it absorbs more sunlight. This extra absorbed heat raises their body temperature faster, getting their muscles working sooner.

items.prompt: What is the main reason a reptile needs to warm up before it can run away from danger?

options.label: To see the predator clearly in bright light
options.feedback: Eyesight works in cold too; the key problem is the muscles and nerves that must be warm to function fast.

options.label: To make its scales smooth for sliding
options.feedback: Scales do not affect running speed; warm muscles and fast nerve signals do.

options.label: Its muscles and nerves work faster when warm
options.feedback: Correct. Warmth speeds up chemical reactions in muscles and nerves, allowing quick, strong movement needed to escape.

options.label: To fill its lungs with enough air
options.feedback: Breathing depth is not the main issue; even with full lungs, cold muscles cannot move quickly.

items.ok_line: Fast escape depends on warm muscles and nerves.
items.ko_line: The real limit is how quickly the body can act, not how well it sees.
items.exp_text: A reptile's cells work through chemical reactions that run faster at higher temperatures. When a reptile is cold, its muscles contract slowly and its nerve signals travel sluggishly. Warming up raises the reaction speed, letting the animal make the sudden burst of movement needed to flee.

items.prompt: What does a basking lizard do to catch more heat from the sun?

options.label: It opens its mouth wide
options.feedback: Opening the mouth may help cool off later, but it does not increase heat absorption from the sun.

options.label: It curls into a tight ball
options.feedback: Curling reduces exposed surface area, so it loses heat, the opposite of what basking aims for.

options.label: It stands on its hind legs
options.feedback: Standing up exposes less body area to heat from below; flattening is the way to gain more heat.

options.label: It flattens its body and turns side-on to the sun
options.feedback: Correct. A flat, wide body facing sideways presents the largest possible surface area to the sun, so it absorbs more heat.

items.ok_line: A flat, side-on body absorbs maximum sunlight.
items.ko_line: Other shapes reduce the area exposed to the sun.
items.exp_text: To warm up efficiently, a lizard spreads its body out flat and turns sideways so its whole side faces the sun. This increases the surface area catching sunlight, letting its body heat up quickly with less time spent basking.
